1002.title: the Ashtavakra Gita complete
1002.hook: the king has just declared himself free, and the sage answers by asking why he still wants money
1002.howItsDone: Some readers of the Ashtavakra Gita take chapters two, three and four together: Janaka's declaration, the sage's testing questions, and Janaka's calm reply, as a model of how a teacher checks a student's realization.

segments.voice: Yesterday, aho: Janaka's cry of wonder, and the waves that turned out to be water. Today, the teacher answers the cry.

What does a good teacher do when a student announces, I've got it? A whole chapter of joy has just poured out of King Janaka: spotless, at peace, salutation to me. Another book might end right there, the student shining and the teacher nodding. The Ashtavakra Gita doesn't. Chapter three opens with the sage leaning in, his tone almost dry. If you really know yourself as the one, imperishable Self, he asks, why are you still keen on piling up wealth? A question aimed straight at a king with a treasury, and at anyone who has made a big announcement about themselves.
screen: `I'VE GOT IT.` → `THE TEACHER LEANS IN.` → `THEN WHY STILL PILE UP WEALTH?`

segments.voice: Much of the third chapter is questions like that, in paraphrase. You know the Self as one and imperishable; why the hunger to get more? Then a picture. Someone on a beach sees a glint in a shell, takes the mother-of-pearl for silver, and a little greed wakes up. The greed is real. The silver isn't. In the same way, he says, wanting for the world rises out of not knowing the Self. Each question pokes a different spot: desire, attachment, the pull of pleasure. Isn't it strange, he keeps asking, that one who knows so much still reaches like this? Some readers find the chapter harsh after the joy before it. On one reading, the test protects the student. Spotless and at peace are easy words to say. The test is whether the hand still closes around the silver. Ashtavakra isn't calling Janaka a liar. He's asking whether the knowing has reached his habits yet, or only his mouth. In the next chapter Janaka answers, calmly: the one who knows the Self moves through the world as though it were a game, not weighed down by it. He doesn't take back what he said. He shows the sage where he stands. A claim, a test, an answer. The wonder of chapter two isn't canceled. It's checked, and checking is part of how this book takes knowledge seriously.

Without judging it, look the way the sage looks at Janaka: silver, or a glint in a shell? Notice where the wanting sits in the body, the chest, the jaw, the hands, breathe into that place, and let the hand open a little.

1003.title: the Ashtavakra Gita complete
1003.hook: a teaching book tells its reader that all the reading won't settle them until they forget it all
1003.howItsDone: Some teachers of the Ashtavakra Gita explain its praise of idleness as the end of inner striving rather than of outward work, and its call to forget everything as letting go of holding the teaching itself as a possession.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shukti and the sage's test: why does the king still reach for silver that's only a shell? Silver, or a shell?

Somewhere on a shelf there's a stack of books about letting go, and every one of them is something else to hold on to. The Ashtavakra Gita seems to know that joke. Deep in the book, the sage says something that could make a diligent reader put the page down. You can talk about the scriptures and listen to them, my child, as much as you like. But you won't rest in yourself until you forget it all. A book telling its reader that the reading isn't the point. And a few verses later, it praises a master of idleness.
screen: `BOOKS ABOUT LETTING GO.` → `FORGET IT ALL.` → `A MASTER OF IDLENESS.`

segments.voice: This is chapter sixteen, in paraphrase. After the line about forgetting, the sage goes on. You may enjoy, you may work, you may meditate, but the mind will still long for what lies beyond all that, where wanting goes quiet. Then something like a diagnosis: everyone is unhappy because of their striving, and nobody notices. Then a verse that can sound like a joke. Happy is the great idler, the one for whom even opening and closing the eyes is a bother. No one else. Read straight, that's a blessing on the couch. The verses around it point another way. Each is about one kind of effort: the strain of the one who thinks I am the doer, the black snake from a few days ago. The great idler isn't someone who won't wash the dishes. It's someone in whom that inner straining has stopped. The dishes may still get washed; nobody inside is clenching about it. Teachers often read the forgetting the same way. The sage isn't asking Janaka to forget his kindness or his duties. He's asking him to stop holding the teaching like a possession, a set of correct ideas to defend. Knowledge carried like luggage is still something extra to carry. Here the book turns on itself, gently: it has spent pages pointing at freedom, and now the pointing has to drop away too. The Vivekachudamani gave a warning like it, about clever talk of scripture, and the Ashtavakra Gita gives it in its own way.
screen: `FORGET IT ALL.` · `UNHAPPY BECAUSE OF STRIVING.` · `THE GREAT IDLER: NO INNER STRAINING.` · `DON'T CARRY THE TEACHING LIKE LUGGAGE.` · then, large: `THE POINTING DROPS AWAY TOO.`

segments.voice: For these minutes, try the sage's kind of idleness: don't manage the breath, don't follow a technique, don't try to remember anything from this week, not even today's lesson. If you catch yourself trying to sit well, let that go too. Whatever is here, let it be here, eyes open or closed, as they like.

Your line: forget it all. Even the teaching can be set down. Day one thousand three, done.

1004.title: the Ashtavakra Gita complete
1004.hook: the last chapter is one small word asked over and over: where?
1004.carry: the medicine has done its work
1004.howItsDone: The Ashtavakra Gita ends with Janaka's chapter of questions beginning with kva, where; some students reread it slowly at the close of their study, asking each where for themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the great idler, in whom the straining stops, and the sage's hardest line: forget it all. Today, the last chapter.
screen: `THE ASHTAVAKRA GITA.` · `FORGET IT ALL.` · `TODAY: THE LAST CHAPTER.`

segments.voice: Kva. In Sanskrit it means where. It's a small word, the kind a child uses looking for a lost shoe. And the last chapter of the Ashtavakra Gita is built almost entirely out of it. Verse after verse, Janaka asks where. Not where is my kingdom, or where did I leave the keys. He asks where the things are that this path spends so long seeking. By the end, the word has asked about nearly everything, and the book simply stops.
screen: `KVA: WHERE.` → `VERSE AFTER VERSE.` → `THEN THE BOOK STOPS.`

segments.voice: Here's the shape of it, in paraphrase. Where are the elements, Janaka asks, where is the body, the senses, the mind, for me, spotless by nature? Where is scripture? Where is knowledge of the Self? Then the line that stops a reader short: where is bondage, and where is liberation? A verse later: where is the karma already begun, where is freedom while living? Those are the very ideas the Vivekachudamani ended on. Bondage and liberation have carried this whole book. Janaka asked about freedom on the first page; the sage told him he was free if he took himself as free. Now, at the end, the student isn't celebrating his freedom. For what he is, even bound and free have nowhere to stand. That's why it's a where and not a no. He isn't saying scripture is wrong or liberation a myth. He looks for them in awareness itself, and finds nothing there that needs them. On this reading, the medicine has done its work, and the bottle can go back on the shelf. So, the book in large steps: a king asks how to be free; a sage says he already is; the king cries out in wonder; the sage tests him; the book says forget even the book; and the king's last word is where. It also closes this year's lineage track, three roads in turn. Karma: the Gita's chapters on action, and a year of service designed. Bhakti: the Gita Govinda, the Bhagavata's tenth book and the kirtan songs. Jnana: the Vivekachudamani and this book. Each with its own voice, none asked to stand in for the others. Tomorrow the path turns to practice again, starting with the breath.
screen: `WHERE IS THE BODY, THE MIND, SCRIPTURE?` · `WHERE IS BONDAGE? WHERE IS LIBERATION?` · `A WHERE, NOT A NO.` · `THE BOOK IN SIX STEPS.` · then, large: `KARMA, BHAKTI, JNANA.`

segments.voice: Borrow Janaka's small word and ask it gently, without hunting for answers. Where is the body? Where is the mind? Where is the one who is trying to be free? After each where, rest in the quiet the question leaves.

1005.title: pranayama sequences
1005.hook: in an Upanishad the body's powers argue over who holds it up, until the breath gets up to leave
1005.carry: like bees with the king bee
1005.howItsDone: Pranayama is traditionally learned from a teacher; in many lineages a session begins sitting upright after some posture work, starting with gentle breath awareness and slow exhalation before any breath retention, and stopping at any dizziness or strain.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ashtavakra Gita ended on one word, kva, where, and the lineage track closed: karma, bhakti, jnana. Today, a new stretch: practices, deeper.

The powers of the body are having an argument. Speech says it holds the body up. The eye says no, it does. The ear, the mind, the elements themselves all make the same boast. It's a scene from the Prashna Upanishad, told by a teacher named Pippalada to a student who asked which powers keep a living being going. In the middle of the shouting, one power gives a single warning and stops arguing. The breath. Prana. Nobody believes it, so it simply gets up, as if to leave.
screen: `THE BODY'S POWERS ARGUE.` → `EACH ONE BOASTS.` → `THE BREATH GETS UP TO LEAVE.`

segments.voice: Here's what happens next, in paraphrase. Prana, the chief power, has warned them: don't be fooled, I'm the one holding this body together. They don't believe it, so prana rises to go. As it rises, every other power is pulled up with it, helpless to stay. When it settles back down, they all settle, like bees that rise when the king bee rises and settle when it settles. The argument is over. Speech, mind, eye and ear turn to prana and praise it. That story sits under this whole week. Pranayama is the name for practices that work with prana by way of the breath. If everything else rises and settles with the breath, then working with the breath works with the rest too: the restless mind, the racing heart, the scattered attention. These days take the practices as sequences, one step after another in an order, gentle ones before stronger ones. Two warnings belong right at the start. Breath practice is done gently: nothing forced, nothing held until it hurts. If there's dizziness or strain, stop and breathe normally. And anyone with a heart or lung condition, or who is pregnant, talks to a doctor before trying the stronger practices. Today there's nothing strong at all. Just the king bee, rising and settling, and everything else going with it.
screen: `PRANA RISES; EVERYTHING RISES.` · `LIKE BEES WITH THE KING BEE.` · `PRANAYAMA: WORKING WITH PRANA.` · `A SEQUENCE: ONE STEP AFTER ANOTHER.` · then, large: `GENTLY. NOTHING FORCED.`

segments.voice: Sit with the spine easy and watch the breath rise and settle without changing it, noticing what goes with it: the belly, the ribs, the shoulders, even the thoughts. After a while, let the out-breath become just a little slower than before, still easy. If anything strains, let it go back to normal.
Pranayama sequences: breath practices set in an order, working with prana, the power the others rise and settle with.
Your line: like bees with the king bee. In the story, when the breath settles, everything settles with it. Day one thousand five.

1006.title: pranayama sequences
1006.hook: in the Yoga Sutra the breath doesn't come first: it waits its turn, after the seat
1006.howItsDone: Where pranayama is taught in this order, it follows posture work: practitioners settle into a steady seat, move through gentle breath practices in a set order, and finish by resting in stillness or meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pranayama sequences began with an Upanishad: the breath rose, and every other power rose with it, like bees with the king bee.
screen: `PRANAYAMA SEQUENCES.` · `LIKE BEES WITH THE KING BEE.`

segments.voice: In Patanjali's Yoga Sutra, the path comes as eight limbs, in order. Restraints. Observances. The seat. Then, fourth in line, pranayama. Then the senses drawn in, then concentration, meditation, absorption. Anyone looking for breathwork might be surprised it isn't first. It waits its turn, after the ways a person treats others and treats themselves, and after the seat, the steady posture. The order is already a sequence, before anyone has counted a single breath.
screen: `EIGHT LIMBS, IN ORDER.` → `PRANAYAMA IS FOURTH.` → `THE BREATH WAITS ITS TURN.`

segments.voice: Here's how the sutras build it, in paraphrase. First the seat: posture should be steady and easy. Not a feat; a way of sitting that can be held without fuss. Once the seat is in place comes pranayama: a pause, a breaking, in the flow of the in-breath and the out-breath. The breath stops running on its own like a tap left open, and comes under gentle attention. Through it, the sutras say, a covering over the inner light grows thin, and the mind becomes fit for concentration. Then the next limb, pratyahara, the senses drawn in. Each step makes the next one possible. A steady seat lets the breath settle. A settled breath lets the mind gather. A gathered mind can turn inward. Skip one and the next wobbles: slowing the breath while the knee aches and the back slumps is hard work, and concentrating with a ragged breath is harder. So a sequence built on this frame starts before the breath, with how a person sits. It moves through breath practices in an order, gentle ones first, and ends by handing over to stillness, not by stopping cold. The sutra doesn't give those exercises one by one; later manuals do. What it gives is the frame: seat, breath, senses, mind, each laid on the last like stones in a path.
screen: `FIRST: A SEAT, STEADY AND EASY.` · `THEN: A PAUSE IN THE FLOW OF BREATH.` · `THE MIND BECOMES FIT TO CONCENTRATE.` · `EACH STEP MAKES THE NEXT POSSIBLE.` · then, large: `SEAT, BREATH, SENSES, MIND.`

segments.voice: Three short steps, the sutra's way. Shift until the sitting feels steady and easy; then let each out-breath slow a little, noticing the small pause at the bottom of it, without holding. Then let the breath find its own pace and rest attention on the touch of air at the nostrils, and if any step wobbles, go back one.
Pranayama sequences: breath practice in an order, starting from a steady seat and ending in a mind gathered enough to turn inward.
Your line: one practice, then the next. In the sutra's order, the seat comes before the breath. That's day one thousand six.

1007.title: pranayama sequences
1007.hook: in the middle of a list of offerings, the Gita slips in the breath itself
1007.howItsDone: Some Hindus who practice pranayama understand it, with Gita 4.29, as an offering in itself, and move through their breath practices in a set order, each one following on from the last.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pranayama sequences in the Yoga Sutra's order: seat, breath, senses, mind. One practice, then the next.

Chapter four of the Bhagavad Gita, and Krishna is making a list. Some offer their sacrifice in fire. Some offer their wealth, some study, some strict vows. It reads like a tour of the ways a person can give something up. Then, tucked into the list, a line that sounds almost like a breathing class. Some offer the in-breath into the out-breath, and the out-breath into the in-breath. No altar, no grain, no butter poured on flames. Just the breath, handed back and forth.
screen: `THE GITA MAKES A LIST.` → `FIRE, WEALTH, STUDY, VOWS.` → `AND THEN: THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: The verse, chapter four, twenty-nine, in paraphrase: some offer the in-breath into the out-breath, and the out-breath into the in-breath, checking the movement of both, devoted to the regulation of breath. That last phrase is pranayama, right there in the Sanskrit, the word carried since the Prashna Upanishad two days ago. Notice the shape. It's already a sequence, the simplest there is: in, then out, then in. But the verse doesn't call it two things. Each half is an offering into the other. The out-breath isn't an ending; it's what the in-breath is given to, and the in-breath is what the out-breath is given to. Around this verse, the chapter keeps widening what counts as sacrifice. A few verses later Krishna says that sacrifice made of knowledge is greater than sacrifice made of things. So a breath practice in this list isn't a warm-up before the real offering. It is one. That changes how a sequence feels from the inside. Moving from a slow count to a gentle pause to a humming breath, each step can finish the last one instead of replacing it. Nothing gets discarded. The quiet from the slow breath is handed to the pause; the pause is handed to the hum. Commentators read the verse in different ways. Some take it as a technical note about holding the breath between in and out. Others read it more widely, as one more inner offering in a chapter full of them. The text leaves room for both. What it does settle is that the breath belongs on the list.
screen: `IN-BREATH OFFERED INTO OUT-BREATH.` · `THE WORD PRANAYAMA IS IN THE VERSE.` · `BREATH COUNTS AS A SACRIFICE.` · `EACH STEP HANDED TO THE NEXT.`

segments.voice: For a few breaths, change nothing; notice where the out-breath ends, and let the next in-breath receive what the last one let go. Then watch the two turning points, out becoming in and in becoming out, without lengthening or holding anything, and after a handful of rounds let the breath carry on by itself. If you pray, you can hold the Gita's picture lightly in mind: breath given into breath.

1008.title: pranayama sequences
1008.hook: a hatha yoga manual compares the breath to a lion, an elephant and a tiger
1008.howItsDone: In some hatha yoga lineages, breath practices are learned in order, gentle ones first, with longer holds left until later and sometimes taught one to one by a teacher who watches the student.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gita's line: in-breath offered into out-breath, each step handed to the next. Breath offered into breath.

A lion, an elephant and a tiger: not the usual cast for a breathing lesson. They turn up in the second chapter of the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, a manual for yogis, right where it starts teaching breath. Nobody walks up to a wild lion on the first day and puts a hand on its head. Taming one goes slowly, a little closer each day. The breath, the text says, is like that. Then it adds a warning that isn't gentle at all.
screen: `A LION, AN ELEPHANT, A TIGER.` → `TAMED A LITTLE AT A TIME.` → `THE BREATH IS LIKE THAT.`

segments.voice: Chapter two, verse fifteen, in paraphrase: as a lion, an elephant or a tiger is brought under control slowly, little by little, so the breath is brought under control. Otherwise, it harms the one who practices. The next verse adds that breath practice done properly helps, and done wrongly brings illness. That's striking from a book that loves breath practice. It isn't warning people off; it's warning them about order. Teachers have a Sanskrit word for the idea, though the verse doesn't use it: krama, a step, going in order. A sequence isn't only a list. It's a decision about what comes first and what has to wait. A few verses earlier, the chapter gives the reason breath matters at all: when the breath moves unsteadily, the mind is unsteady; when the breath is still, the mind is still. The breath is a way in to the mind, so the manual treats it the way a keeper treats a big animal. Some teachers in the hatha tradition begin with slow breathing and simple counting, and leave long holds for later, sometimes learned one to one with someone watching. This week has followed that line: the breath the others rise with, the seat before the breath, breath offered into breath, and now the pace. The week began with the Ashtavakra Gita, a text about a self already free, and the two pull in different directions. At one point the sage tells Janaka that practicing meditation is itself his bondage; the hatha manual is practice from start to finish. The tradition has kept both books, and some teachers read both.
screen: `TAMED LITTLE BY LITTLE.` · `DONE WRONGLY, IT HARMS.` · `UNSTEADY BREATH, UNSTEADY MIND.` · `GENTLE FIRST, LONG HOLDS LATER.`

segments.voice: Start with a few breaths as they come, then a gentle count: in for four, out for four. When that's easy, stretch only the out-breath to five or six, and if the chest, throat or jaw strains, return to the even count; that return is part of the sequence, not a failure of it. Near the end, drop the counting and let the breath settle by itself.
Pranayama sequences. Breath practices set in an order. Today, the pace of that order: little by little, the way a keeper tames a lion.
Your line: little by little. The keeper doesn't rush the lion, and neither does the manual. See you tomorrow.
